A lamp shines on a metal plate. What decides whether electrons fly off — brightness or colour?

About: Photoelectric Effect

Source

Topic
Quantum physics — the photoelectric effect (Einstein, 1905)
Concept
Light delivers energy in discrete quanta of size hf; ejection requires hf ≥ φ regardless of intensity.
Serves
Predicting the threshold frequency, distinguishing intensity from frequency, seeing that frequency alone sets K_max through K_max = hf − φ.
Key inquiry
Why can a dim blue lamp eject electrons while a bright red one cannot?
Misconception
“More intense light ⇒ more energetic electrons.” (Reality: more intense ⇒ more electrons, same K_max.)

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict — a bright red lamp

Red light of frequency f = 4.3×10¹⁴ Hz falls on a sodium plate, and the beam is turned up to full brightness. Are electrons ejected?

2 · Observe — same brightness, higher frequency

The lamp is now violet, f = 8.0×10¹⁴ Hz, at the same brightness as before. Compare the plate with the red case: what has changed, and what has not?

One photon carries energy hf. Sodium's work function is φ = 2.28 eV.

3 · Predict — faster electrons

The ejected electrons leave with a maximum kinetic energy K_max. To make them leave faster, what has to change?

4 · Predict — swap the metal

The plate is cesium, φ = 2.10 eV, and electrons are streaming off. Leaving the lamp exactly as it is, you swap the plate for zinc, φ = 4.30 eV. What happens?

5 · What the experiment shows

Four observations, none of them explicable by waves: nothing is emitted below f₀ = φ/h however bright the lamp; K_max = hf − φ is set by frequency alone; brightness sets only the number of electrons per second; and emission begins the instant the light arrives.

In the laboratory K_max is measured as a stopping potential: the reverse voltage V₀ that just turns back the fastest electrons, eV₀ = K_max. Einstein's 1905 explanation of these four facts won the 1921 Nobel Prize.

01

At a glance

A lamp shines light of a chosen frequency and brightness onto a metal plate. The sim follows the light, the electrons held in the metal and anything that leaves it.

What you'll learn

  • How much energy one photon of light carries, and which setting controls it.
  • What the work function φ of a metal is, and how it gives each metal a threshold frequency.
  • How frequency, brightness and the choice of metal each show up in what the plate does.
Photons travel from the lamp to the plate. The blue dots are electrons bound in the metal.

What's on screen

  • Photons: wavy lines from the lamp. Their colour follows the frequency.
  • Plate: shows the metal's name and φ, with blue dots for its bound electrons.
  • Ejected e⁻: green dots with a straight track, one at a time tagged with a K value.
  • Numbers: f and hf under the lamp, and hf and φ at the bottom left. Live Readouts lists the rest.
See itStart with sodium at the opening settings. Watch for: wavy photon lines crossing from the lamp to the plate, and the plate labelled with its name and φ.

The lamp sends one frequency at a time. In the sim every photon that can free an electron does so, and every freed electron carries the same K.

03

One photon carries the energy hf

Einstein proposed in 1905 that light arrives in packets called photons. A photon of frequency f carries the energy

Ephoton = hf
h is Planck's constant.

Atomic energies are quoted in electron-volts, where 1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J. In these units h = 4.136×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s, so every 10¹⁴ Hz on the frequency slider adds 0.4136 eV to each photon. The slider range, 3.5 to 12 ×10¹⁴ Hz, spans photons of 1.45 to 4.96 eV.

A beam is a stream of identical photons. Frequency sets the energy of each one. Intensity sets how many photons leave the lamp every second.

See itSet sodium with the frequency at 6.0 ×10¹⁴ Hz. Watch for: hf = 2.48 eV under the lamp and in the readouts, from 6.0 × 0.4136.
04

An electron leaves only if one photon has hf at least φ

Electrons in a metal are bound to it. The work function φ is the least energy needed to pull one out, and each metal has its own value. At lamp intensities an electron takes in one photon at a time and cannot add up energy from several. So an electron can leave only if a single photon has hf ≥ φ. That sets a threshold frequency:

f0 = φ / h
The lowest frequency that can free an electron from that metal.

Below f₀ every photon falls short. A brighter lamp only sends more photons that each fall short, so nothing leaves.

Metalφ (eV)f₀ (×10¹⁴ Hz)
Cesium2.105.08
Sodium2.285.51
Calcium2.876.94
Zinc4.3010.40
Copper4.7011.36
See itUse sodium at 5.0 ×10¹⁴ Hz and full intensity. Watch for: photons landing on the plate, but no green electrons, with hf = 2.07 eV under φ = 2.28 eV.
05

The leftover energy is the electron's kinetic energy

A photon hands all of hf to one electron. Getting out of the metal costs at least φ, and whatever is left over is kinetic energy. The fastest electrons lose nothing else on the way out, so

Kmax = hf − φ
Einstein's photoelectric equation.

Frequency enters through hf and the metal through φ. In the lab, Kmax is found as the stopping potential V₀, the reverse voltage that just turns the fastest electrons back, so eV₀ = Kmax. The V₀ readout is Kmax in volts. Real electrons can lose energy inside the metal, which is why Kmax is a maximum. The sim gives every electron exactly this value.

f (×10¹⁴ Hz)hf (eV)Kmax on sodium (eV)
6.02.480.20
8.03.311.03
10.04.141.86

Read from the sim's own controls.

See itUse sodium at 8.0 ×10¹⁴ Hz. Watch for: a green electron tagged K = 1.03 eV, which is 3.31 − 2.28, and V₀ = 1.03 V.
06

Brightness sets how many electrons leave, not how fast

The intensity slider sets how many photons reach the plate each second. When hf ≥ φ, each photon frees one electron in the sim, so the ejection rate follows the intensity. Doubling the brightness doubles the rate. Every electron still gets hf − φ, so Kmax stays put. Real metals free an electron for only a small fraction of photons, but the rate still follows the intensity. Real emission also starts the instant light arrives, even when dim. The sim does not show that timescale.

See itUse sodium at 8.0 ×10¹⁴ Hz and full intensity. Watch for: an ejection rate near 60 /s, twice the rate at 50 %, while the K tags still read 1.03 eV.

The metal changes φ and so f₀, but not hf. The same lamp can free electrons from one metal and none from another.

See itUse zinc at 6.0 ×10¹⁴ Hz and full intensity. Watch for: no electrons leave, because hf = 2.48 eV is under zinc's φ = 4.30 eV. Zinc needs f₀ = 10.40.
07

Where it matters

  • Photocells and light meters. Photons freeing electrons give a current that grows with the brightness, because the electron count follows the photon count.
  • Photomultiplier tubes. A photocathode turns single photons into single electrons, which the tube then multiplies into a pulse big enough to count.
  • Solar cells and camera sensors. They use a related effect inside a semiconductor, where a photon must carry at least the energy gap to free an electron. Light below that threshold does nothing, however bright.
08

Summary

In one line. A photon's energy hf and the metal's work function φ together set what the plate does.

Key points

  • A photon carries hf. Frequency sets that energy, and intensity sets how many photons arrive.
  • An electron leaves only if one photon has hf ≥ φ, that is f ≥ f₀ = φ/h.
  • Kmax = hf − φ, and eV₀ = Kmax.
  • Intensity changes the number of electrons per second, not Kmax.

Common mix-ups

  • "A bright enough red lamp will eject electrons in the end." Brightness adds photons, and each one still carries too little energy. Below f₀ nothing leaves.
  • "Brighter light gives faster electrons." It gives more electrons per second, with the same Kmax.
  • "A metal with a larger φ just gives slower electrons." If hf is under φ it gives none at all.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict Kmax for sodium at 7.0 ×10¹⁴ Hz, then check the readout.
  • Find the lowest frequency at which cesium ejects electrons, and compare it with 5.08.
  • Find the frequency at which copper starts to eject electrons at full intensity.
